1.  The present accident claim is based on a detailed accident Digitally signed by CHARU CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date:

2. The brief facts of the case are that on 29.08.2018, on receipt of DD no.9A, SI Ajit Singh reached BRT Road (under Chirag Delhi Flyover),where he found a Hero Splendor motorcycle no.
DL-3SDG-3727 and a Taxi bearing no. DFL- 1RTA-7525(hereinafter referred to as offending vehicle)
in accidental condition. On receipt of information, IO reached AIIMS Trauma Center where he met the victim/injured Krishna Gupta who stated that on 29.08.2018 he was going on his motorcycle towards Safdarjung hospital. At 8 AM he reached under the Chirag Delhi Flyover and signal on his side was green. When he broke on the BRT road, the offending vehicle suddenly came from the side Krishna Gupta vs Devender (146/18, G.K. ) on 5 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20607102/
1 of the Red light, driven in rash and negligent manner and hit the motorcycle of the petitioner. 
Relative of the petitioner namely Manoj Gupta was also a pillion rider on the motorcycle of the petitioner. As an impact of the accident, both the petitioner and his relative fell resulting in injury to the petitioner while his relative did not sustain any injury. 
3. An FIR no.146 of 2018 dated 29.08.2018 was registered u/s 279,338 of IPC at PS Greater Kailash-I and the matter was investigated. After investigation a charge sheet was filed before concerned criminal court against the driver of the offending vehicle(Respondent no.1) while DAR was filed before this Tribunal. 
4. Respondent no.1 is driver-cum-owner of offending vehicle, and Respondent no.2 is the insurance company with which the offending vehicle was insured. CHARU GUPTA Date:
by CHARU GUPTA 2024.11.05 16:00:19 +0530 MACT NO:1023/18 Krishna Gupta v.
Devender P.No. 2 Of 19 BK 5. In response to the DAR, a legal offer was filed by Respondent no.2, however, Respondent no.2 also sought 40% deduction in the compensation amount on account of contributory negligence on the part of the petitioner for having failed to show that he was holding a valid driving licence on the date of accident. 
No reply/written statement was filed by Respondent no.1 despite opportunity. 
6. After completion of pleadings, following issues were framed on 06.12.2018 1. Whether the injured Krishna Gupta suffered injuries in a road traffic accident on 29.08.2018 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no. DL-1RTA-7525 (Dzire car) being driven and owned by R1and insured with R2? OPP. 
2. Whether the injured is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? OPP. 
3. Relief.
7. In the present case, despite numerous opportunities, petitioner chose not to lead any evidence. 
Petitioner stopped appearing before the court, due to which matter was dismissed in default for non-prosecution vide order dated 06.01.2022. The same was later revived on an application moved by the petitioner, vide order dated 31.08.2022. Vide order dated 01.08.2019, interest of the petitioner was closed from the date of framing of issues till leading of evidence. Since no evidence has been led, petitioner is not entitled to any interest in terms of order dated 01.08.2019. 
Subsequently, vide order dated 05.09.2023, opportunity of petitioner to lead evidence was also closed. Digitally signed by CHARU CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date:
2024.11.05 16:00:28 +0530 MACT NO:1023/18 Krishna Gupta v. Devender P.No. 3 Of 19 BK Respondents also did not lead any evidence.

2 8. Final arguments in detail were addressed on behalf of the claimant and the insurance company. It is argued by learned counsel for petitioner that since the present claim arises out of a DAR, the contents thereof and the documents annexed therewith may be read and considered by the Tribunal to decide the compensation payable to the petitioner since Respondent no.2 has not challenged negligence on the part of Respondent no.1 by filing a legal offer. 
On the other hand, it is the argument of learned counsel for insurance company that without any evidence being led, petitioner cannot claim compensation. It is further argued that a deduction of 40% or more may be made towards contributory negligence as the claimant has suffered accident at the time when he attempted to jump the red light. 
On the basis of pleadings/DAR on record and arguments addressed, issue wise findings are as under:
Whether the injured Krishna Gupta suffered injuries in a road traffic accident on 29.08.2018 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no. DL-1RTA-7525 (Dzire car) being driven and owned by R1and insured with R2? OPP. 
9. Before proceeding to decide the above issue, it is apposite to note that as a settled principle of law, proceedings under The Motor Vehicle Act are not considered akin to the proceedings in a civil suit and hence strict rules of evidence are not applicable.
Reliance is placed upon decision in Bimla Devi & ors. vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation &
Ors. (2009) 13 SC 535, Digitally signed by CHARU CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date:
2024.11.05 16:00:38 +0530 MACT NO:1023/18 Krishna Gupta v. Devender P.No. 4 Of 19 BK in Parmeshwari vs. Amir Chand & Ors., 2011 (1) SCR 1096 and National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana, 2009 ACJ 287, wherein it has been held that the negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view has to be taken.
10. Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Rajesh Tyagi & Ors. v. Jaibir Singh & Ors.(FAO No.842/2003, decided on 08.01.2021), observed:
"...13.14. It is not always that if issues have been framed, further evidence is required. 
The matter can be disposed of after hearing the arguments based on the material on record or some evidence on a specific point may be called for. In any inquiry, there is also a duty of the Court to see that the evidence which could have been brought is brought so that justice is done..." 
In the present case, though issues had been framed, it is noteworthy that the insurance company has placed a legal offer instead of a specific defence denying rash or negligent conduct on the part of the drive of the offending vehicle. Hence, it is assumed that the insurance company accepts/admits the Krishna Gupta vs Devender (146/18, G.K. ) on 5 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20607102/
3 factum of negligence and rashness on the part of the offending vehicle. In such circumstances,
petitioner cannot be bound to lead evidence to prove a fact which the insurance company has not specifically disputed. Rather in the legal offer filed by the insurance company a defence of contributory negligence on the part of petitioner has been raised by pleading that the petitioner was also rash and negligent in so far as he was crossing (jumping) the red light at the time of the accident and also that he has not filed his driving licence on record showing that he was CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.11.05 16:00:49 +0530 MACT NO:1023/18 Krishna Gupta v.
Devender P.No. 5 Of 19 BK riding a motorcycle without a valid driving licence. It is pertinent to note that even as per the DAR filed by the investigating officer, accident has occurred at the crossing where a traffic light was also installed. As per the DAR, the petitioner contributed to the accident by being negligent in keeping to the left side of the road and by maintaining an excessive speed. 
Petitioner has failed to produce his driving licence to rebut the plea of riding a motorcycle without holding a valid driving licence. At the same time, it has been held in Dinesh Kumar v. National Insurance Company Ltd.(2018) 1 SCC 750 that mere absence of driving licence with the injured or deceased would not amount to contributory negligence. 
Further, since there is no evidence to show that the petitioner either jumped the red light or was at an excessively high speed, no contributory negligence qua such plea can be assumed. Further, since the accident has taken place at almost the center point of a junction, it cannot be said that the petitioner failed to keep on his left side. As such, no deduction can be made on the ground of contributory negligence. 
11. In the present case, the driver-cum-owner of the offending vehicle has neither filed any written statement nor has led any evidence to dispute occurrence of the accident owing to his rash or negligent driving. In fact, filing of the chargesheet against such driver-cum-owner by the investigating officer u/s 279/338 of IPC is itself suggestive of rash and negligent driving by such driver of the offending vehicle. Further, the fact that the police after investigation had filed charge-sheet against Respondent no.1 under section 279,338,304A of IPC is also suggestive of CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.11.05 16:00:57 +0530 MACT NO:1023/18 Krishna Gupta v. Devender P.No. 6 Of 19 BK negligence on the part of Respondent no.1. Reliance is placed on the decision in National Insurance Co. Vs. Pushpa Rana 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, wherein it was laid down that completion of investigation and filing of chargesheet are sufficient proof of negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle.
12. In totality of circumstances, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner have been able to prove on the scales of preponderance of probabilities that the accident in question took place due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by its driver/respondent no.1 on the date and time of accident. Accordingly, issue no.1 is decided in favour of petitioner and against the respondents. 
Issue no. 2 Whether the injured is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom? OPP.

4 13. As discussed in issue no.1, petitioner is entitled to compensation. Since no statutory defence has been raised by the insurance company, insurance company is liable to compensate the petitioner. 
14. As regards the quantum of compensation, this court is governed by the law laid down by Hon'le Supreme Court in Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 Supreme Court cases 343, Sarla Verma & Ors. v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Ors. (2003) 6SCC 121 and National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi & Ors.(2017) 16 SCC 680. The gist of the law is that the object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a CHARU GUPTA Date:
GUPTA 2024.11.05 16:01:09 +0530 MACT NO:1023/18 Krishna Gupta v. Devender P.No. 7 Of 19 BK fair, reasonable and equitable manner. The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable. A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury. This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned. 
15. Further it can be noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability. 
(iii) Future medical expenses. 
Non-pecuniary damages (General damages) 
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries. 
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of Digitally signed CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA 2024.11.05 Date:

5 16:01:40 +0530 MACT NO:1023/18 Krishna Gupta v. Devender P.No. 8 Of 19 BK marriage).
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
15.1. In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii) (a)
and (iv). 15.2. It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii),
(v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
15.3. Assessment of pecuniary damages under Item (i) and under Item (ii) (a) do not pose much difficulty as they involve reimbursement of actuals and are easily ascertainable from the evidence. 
15.4. Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for further treatment and cost thereof.
15.5. Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves determination of l u m p s u m a m o u n t s w i t h r e f e r e n c e t o c i r c u m s t a n c e s s u c h a s a g e , n a t u r e o f injury/deprivation/disability suffered by the claimant and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant. Decisions of Hon'ble SC and Hon'ble High Courts contain necessary guidelines for award under these heads, if necessary. 15.6. It was observed by Hon'ble Sc in such case of Raj Kumar (supra) that what usually poses some difficulty is the assessment Digitally signed CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date:
2024.11.05 16:01:49 +0530 MACT NO:1023/18 Krishna Gupta v. Devender P.No. 9 Of 19 BK of the loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability --Item (ii) (a).
15.7. We are not concerned with assessment regarding loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability in this case, as petitioner did not suffer any permanent disability. 
16. As per record, Aadhar card of the injured/petitioner, date of birth of petitioner is 06.08.1995. Same has not been disputed. 
Accident occurred on 29.08.2018. As such, petitioner would have been about 23 years at the time of accident.

6 As per MLC of the injured prepared at Jai Prakash Narain Apex Trauma Center and the discharge summary prepared at VMMC and Safdarjung hospital, New Delhi, injured was diagnosed with closed traumatic fracture BB leg (R). He was admitted in Trauma Center on 29.08.2018 and transferred/ referred on the same day to Safdarjung hospital. As per record, the injured also underwent surgery at Safdarjung hospital on 06.09.2018 and was discharged on 08.09.2018. As per discharge summary prepared at the VMMC and Safdarjung hospital injured remained hospitalized for the purpose of surgery from 05.09.2018 till 08.09.2018. Thus, keeping note of the fact that the petitioner suffered a fracture, the injury has to be treated as grievous injury. 
17. Petitioner has filed photocopies of certain medical bills which are unverified and no original thereof have ever been produced. As such, none of these bills can be considered for the purpose of compensation towards medical expenses. However, considering the nature of injury and the general medical expense required by any person of the age of injured, it is assumed that CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date:
2024.11.05 16:01:59 +0530 MACT NO:1023/18 Krishna Gupta v. Devender P.No. 10 Of 19 BK the injured may have expended about Rs.15,000/- towards his treatment. 
As such, Rs.15,000/- is awarded towards medical expenses incurred. 
18. As regards loss of earning of petitioner, it first needs to be ascertained the nature of job and salary/wages drawn by petitioner at the time of accident. Petitioner has claimed to be working as a driver at the time of accident and drawing a salary of Rs.15,000/-p.m.,however no evidence has been lead to prove his employment or salary. No proof of educational qualification or even a driving licence, to prove that he could have worked as a driver has been produced. As such, income of the injured has to be assessed as per minimum wages of an unskilled labour. 
Having regard to the medical documents showing the period of hospitalization and the nature of injury suffered, it is assumed that the petitioner may have been incapacitated from working for at least one month. Accordingly, petitioner is entitled to compensation towards loss of income for one month. 
As per minimum wages of an unskilled labour at Delhi, at the time of accident were Rs.13,896/-. 
Hence, the same is granted towards loss of income. 
He is also entitled to attendant charges for the said period i.e. Rs.10,000/-. 
No compensation towards future loss of income can be granted in cases where petitioner has not proved to have sustained any permanent disability.

23. Another issue which is to be decided is out of such Award amount, how much is to be released at present and how much is to kept in the form of FDR for future financial used of the petitioner. 
24. At this stage, it is relevant to the refer to the judgment of A. V. Padma & Ors. Vs.,
R. Venugopal & Ors. (2012) 3 Supreme Court Cases 378:
" ......In the case of Susamma Thomas (supra), this Court issued certain guidelines in order to "safeguard the feed from being frittered away by the beneficiaries due to ignorance, illiteracy and susceptibility to exploitation". 
Even as per the guidelines issued by this Court Court, long term fixed deposit of amount of compensation is mandatory only in the case of Digitally signed CHARU by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.11.05 16:03:14 +0530 MACT NO:1023/18 Krishna Gupta v. Devender P.No. 15 Of 19 BK minors, illiterate claimants and widows. In the case of illiterate claimants, the Tribunal is allowed to consider the request for lumpsum payment for effecting purchase of any movable property such as agricultural implements, rickshaws etc. to earn a living. However, in such cases, the Tribunal shall make sure that the amount is actually spent for the purpose and the demand is not a ruse to withdraw money. In the case of semi-illiterate claimants, the Tribunal should ordinarily invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. But if the Tribunal is satisfied for reasons to be Krishna Gupta vs Devender (146/18, G.K. ) on 5 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/20607102/
10 stated in writing that the whole or part of the amount is required for expanding an existing business or for purchasing some property for earning a livelihood, the Tribunal can release the whole or part of the amount of compensation to the claimant provided the Tribunal will ensure that the amount is invested for the purpose for which it is demanded and paid. In the case of literate persons, it is not mandatory to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. 
The expression used in guideline No. (iv) issued by this Court is that in the case of literate persons also the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i), whereas in the guideline Nos.
(i), (ii), (iii) and (v), the expression used is that the Tribunal should. Moreover, in the case of literate persons, the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i) only if, having regard to the age, fiscal background and strata of the society to which the claimant belongs and such other considerations, the Tribunal thinks that in the larger interest of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded, it is necessary to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit. 
Thus, sufficient discretion has been given to the Tribunal not to insist on investment of the compensation amount in long term fixed deposit CHARU Digitally signed by CHARU GUPTA GUPTA Date: 2024.11.05 16:03:28 +0530 MACT NO:1023/18 Krishna Gupta v. Devender P.No. 16 Of 19 BK and to release even the whole amount in the case of literate persons. However, the Tribunals are often taking a very rigid stand and are mechanically ordering in almost all cases that the amount of compensation shall be invested in long term fixed deposit. They are taking such a rigid and mechanical approach without understanding and appreciating the distinction drawn by this Court in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows and in the case of semiliterate and literate persons. It needs to be clarified that the above guidelines were issued by this Court only to safeguard the interests of the claimants, particularly the minors, illiterates and others whose amounts are sought to be withdrawn on some fictitious grounds. The guidelines were not to be understood to mean that the Tribunals were to take a rigid stand while considering an application seeking release of the money. 
The guidelines cast a responsibility on the Tribunals to pass appropriate orders after examining each case on its own merits. However, it is seen that even in cases when there is no possibility or chance of the feed being frittered away by the beneficiary owing to ignorance, illiteracy or susceptibility to exploitation, investment of the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit is directed by the Tribunals as a matter of course and in a routine manner, ignoring the object and the spirit of the guidelines issued by this Court and the genuine requirements of the claimants. Even in the case of literate persons, the Tribunals are automatically ordering investment of the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit without recording that having regard to the age or fiscal background or the strata of the society to which the claimant belongs or such other considerations,
